questions.q: Which question does authorization (as opposed to authentication) answer?
choices: Is this user allowed to perform this action?
Is this user really who they claim to be?
Was this password typed by a human rather than a script?
Has this session cookie expired?
questions.explain: Authentication verifies identity. Authorization decides what that authenticated user may do, so permissions are checked after authentication.

questions.q: Which of these are inherence factors ("something you are or do")?
choices: A fingerprint scan
Typing or behavior patterns
A hardware security token
The answer to a security question
questions.explain: Inherence factors are biometrics and behavior patterns. A security token is a possession factor, and a security question answer is a knowledge factor.

questions.q: A phone that receives or generates a one-time login code is an example of which factor type?
choices: Possession factor
Knowledge factor
Inherence factor
Authorization factor
questions.explain: It is "something you have", which makes it a possession factor.

questions.q: Compromising a low-privilege account has no security impact beyond that one user's own data.
questions.explain: Even a low-privilege account can expose sensitive business data. It also gives the attacker extra attack surface, because internal pages allow attacks that public pages don't.

questions.q: Logic flaws or poor coding that let an attacker bypass the authentication mechanism entirely are commonly called ________.
questions.explain: Auth vulnerabilities come from either weak brute-force protection or logic flaws that allow a bypass. The second kind is called broken authentication.

questions.q: A site requires a minimum length, mixed case and a special character. Why can targeted guesses like "Mypassword1!" still succeed?
choices: Users bend a memorable password to fit the policy in predictable ways
Complexity policies are never enforced on the server
Special characters are stripped before hashing
Mixed case is ignored when passwords are compared
questions.explain: The policy gives high entropy only in theory. People turn "mypassword" into "Mypassword1!" or "Myp4$$w0rd" and make small edits when forced to change it, so educated guesses beat trying every combination.

questions.q: When a login attempt uses a valid username but a wrong password, which differences in the response could reveal that the username exists?
choices: A different HTTP status code
A different error message, even by one character
A noticeably different response time
Whether the login form is submitted with POST
questions.explain: Status codes, error messages and response times can all leak username validity. The form's HTTP method is the same no matter which username is entered.

questions.q: Two error messages that differ by one character that isn't visible on the rendered page can still allow username enumeration.
questions.explain: Any difference in the response, even a typo or an invisible character, can be detected and used to tell valid usernames from invalid ones.

questions.q: When testing for username enumeration through response times, why submit an excessively long password?
choices: It makes the extra processing for valid usernames take noticeably longer
It overflows the username field
It forces the server to return a different status code
It bypasses account locking
questions.explain: If the password is only checked when the username is valid, a very long password makes that extra work take longer, so the timing difference stands out.

questions.q: In HTTP basic authentication, the username and password are joined with a colon and then encoded with which scheme?
questions.explain: The Base64 token is sent in the "Authorization: Basic <token>" header on every request. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.

questions.q: Why is HTTP basic authentication generally considered insecure?
choices: Credentials go with every request, so they can be captured in transit unless the site uses HSTS
It often has no brute-force protection, and the token is just static values
It provides no CSRF protection on its own
It stores a salted one-way hash that is slow to verify
questions.explain: Basic auth resends static, reversible credentials with every request, often lacks brute-force protection and has no CSRF protection. It does not use salted hashing.

questions.q: A site blocks an IP after too many failed logins, but the failed-attempt counter resets after any successful login from that IP. Why is this a weakness?
choices: An attacker can mix logins to their own valid account into the guesses to keep resetting the counter
Successful logins reveal the victim's password
The block applies to the victim instead of the attacker
It causes the server to return a different status code for valid usernames
questions.explain: Adding the attacker's own valid credentials to the guess list at regular intervals stops the counter from ever reaching the limit, so the defense does nothing.

questions.q: Account locking mainly protects against which kind of attack?
choices: Targeted brute-forcing of one specific account
Trying a few common passwords against many accounts
Credential stuffing with leaked username/password pairs
Session hijacking with a stolen cookie
questions.explain: Locking stops many guesses against one account. It does not stop an attacker who tries only a few passwords per account across many usernames, staying under the limit.

questions.q: An "account locked" response can itself help an attacker enumerate valid usernames.
questions.explain: Only existing accounts can be locked, so a lock message confirms the username is valid.

questions.q: Why doesn't account locking stop credential stuffing?
choices: Each username is tried only once, with its leaked password
Credential stuffing uses only the admin account
Locked accounts are automatically unlocked by a CAPTCHA
Credential stuffing targets the registration form instead of login
questions.explain: Credential stuffing replays real username/password pairs from data breaches, relying on password reuse. One attempt per username never trips a lock, and one automated run can compromise many accounts.

questions.q: User rate limiting is sometimes preferred over account locking because it is less prone to username enumeration and denial of service.
questions.explain: Rate limiting blocks the requester's IP instead of locking the account, so legitimate users aren't locked out and no lock message reveals which accounts exist.

questions.q: Under typical user rate limiting, how can a blocked IP become unblocked?
choices: Automatically, after some time passes
Manually, by an administrator
By the user completing a CAPTCHA
By submitting the login form with a different username
questions.explain: Blocks are lifted by time passing, an admin, or a CAPTCHA. Changing the username doesn't help because the block applies to the IP.

questions.q: Why is a password followed by a code sent by email not true two-factor authentication?
choices: It checks the knowledge factor twice, because getting the code only takes the email login credentials
Email codes are always too short
Email cannot carry numeric codes reliably
It checks the inherence factor instead of the possession factor
questions.explain: Real MFA must verify different factors. Access to the code depends on knowing the email credentials, so it is another knowledge factor.

questions.q: Why are SMS verification codes weaker than codes generated by a dedicated authenticator app or device?
choices: The code is transmitted to the phone instead of generated on it, so it can be intercepted
SIM swapping lets an attacker receive the victim's SMS messages
SMS codes are a knowledge factor rather than a possession factor
SMS codes cannot expire
questions.explain: SMS is technically "something you have", but sending the code opens it to interception, and SIM swapping hands the victim's number to the attacker.

questions.q: When the password and the verification code are entered on separate pages, a site may treat the user as logged in before the second step is completed.
questions.explain: If logged-in-only pages don't check that the second step was completed, the 2FA step can be skipped entirely. This should be tested.

questions.q: After step 1 of login, a site sets a cookie like account=carlos, and step 2 uses that cookie to decide which account the verification code is for. What is the core flaw?
choices: The server doesn't check that the same user who passed step 1 is completing step 2
The verification code is too long
The cookie is sent over HTTPS
Step 1 uses POST instead of GET
questions.explain: Because step 2 trusts a client-controlled cookie, the second factor isn't tied to the user who passed the first. Combined with weak code protection, the password check becomes meaningless.

questions.q: Logging the user out after a few wrong verification codes reliably stops automated guessing of 2FA codes.
questions.explain: Tools can automate the multi-step re-login, for example Burp Intruder macros or Turbo Intruder, so the logout only slows the attack.

questions.q: How many possible values does a 4-digit numeric verification code have?
questions.explain: 10^4 = 10,000 (0000 to 9999). Without proper limits, that is a trivially small space to guess through.

questions.q: A "remember me" cookie is the Base64 encoding of the username and a timestamp. Why is this insecure?
choices: Base64 is reversible encoding, so the structure is easy to recover and forge for other users
Base64 cookies cannot be persistent
Timestamps make the cookie expire too quickly
Browsers refuse to send Base64 cookies over HTTPS
questions.explain: The cookie bypasses login entirely, so it must be impractical to guess. A predictable mix of static values plus reversible encoding gives no protection.

questions.q: Why does salting matter if a hashed password ends up in a cookie?
choices: Without a salt, the hash can be matched against precomputed hashes of common passwords to recover the cleartext
Salt makes the hash reversible for the server
Salt shortens the cookie so it fits in the header
Unsalted hashes cannot be stored in cookies
questions.explain: Hashes of common passwords are widely available online, so an unsalted hash of a common password can often be cracked offline just by looking it up.

questions.q: Which properties should a password-reset URL token have?
choices: High entropy, so it is hard to guess
It gives no hint of which user it belongs to
It expires quickly and is destroyed right after the reset
It contains the username so the back end can find the account
questions.explain: The back end should look up which user a token belongs to. The token itself shouldn't reveal or be built from the username, as in /reset-password?user=victim-user.

questions.q: A site checks the reset token when the reset page is loaded but not when the new-password form is submitted. Why is this dangerous?
choices: The token can be removed from the submission, letting the form reset other users' passwords
The new password will be stored in plaintext
The token will expire too early
The user will be logged out of all sessions
questions.explain: The token must be re-validated when the form is submitted. Otherwise the check that protects the reset can simply be skipped.

questions.q: What is the attack called in which a dynamically generated password-reset URL is manipulated (for example through the Host header) so that the victim's reset token is sent to the attacker?
questions.explain: Password reset poisoning abuses how the reset link is built, so the attacker can capture the token and change the victim's password.

questions.q: Emailing users a newly generated password is safe as long as the password is random.
questions.explain: It is a persistent password sent over an insecure channel. Inboxes are persistent and often synced over insecure channels, so it is risky unless the password expires very quickly or must be changed right away.

questions.q: A password-change form carries the target username in a hidden field and can be used without being logged in as that user. What does this expose?
choices: Username enumeration and password brute-forcing for any account, through the change form
Only the attacker's own account
Nothing, because hidden fields cannot be edited
Cross-site scripting in the password field
questions.explain: Hidden fields are client-controlled. The change form runs the same username/password check as login, so it can be aimed at any user.

questions.q: Name the JavaScript real-time password strength estimator developed by Dropbox.
questions.explain: Rather than relying on traditional composition rules, accept only passwords that a strength checker like zxcvbn rates highly.

questions.q: Which measures help prevent username enumeration on a login page?
choices: Truly identical, generic error messages
The same HTTP status code for every failed login
Response times that can't be told apart
A specific "username not found" message to help legitimate users
questions.explain: Any observable difference, whether in message, status code or timing, leaks whether an account exists.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to make sure login credentials are never sent over an unencrypted connection?
choices: Redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS
Base64-encode the password before sending it
Use HTTP basic authentication
Hash the password in a cookie
questions.explain: Forcing HTTPS with redirects protects credentials in transit. Encoding like Base64 gives no confidentiality.

questions.q: Robust IP-based rate limiting with CAPTCHAs completely eliminates the risk of brute-force attacks.
questions.explain: It won't eliminate brute-forcing. The goal is to make it tedious and manual enough that attackers move to a softer target.

questions.q: Which second factor is considered the ideal choice for MFA?
choices: A dedicated device or app that generates the code itself
A code sent by email
A code sent by SMS
A second security question
questions.explain: Email codes are long-winded single-factor auth, SMS is vulnerable to SIM swapping, and a second security question is the same factor again.

questions.q: In some applications, merely revealing that a particular person has an account is sensitive information.
questions.explain: This is one reason preventing username enumeration matters beyond making brute-forcing harder.
